readerTitle: Why well-run companies lose to worse products
caseNote: 실제 연구·산업 사례 (Christensen의 굴착기 산업 분석) + 가상 적용 (회계 소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 기존 강자는 게을러서가 아니라 '좋은 경영'의 규칙을 충실히 따르기 때문에 와해적 제품을 놓친다.
misconception: 큰 회사가 신생 기업에 지는 이유는 오만하거나, 기술을 몰랐거나, 경영을 잘못했기 때문이다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press. (Chapter 3: the mechanical excavator industry)
Bower, J. L. & Christensen, C. M. (1995). Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave. Harvard Business Review.
King, A. A. & Baatartogtokh, B. (2015). How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation? MIT Sloan Management Review.
Lepore, J. (2014). The Disruption Machine. The New Yorker.

factChecks.note: 굴착기 사례의 시기(2차 대전 이후 유압식 등장, 1970년대 무렵 주류 대체)는 Christensen(1997) 3장으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도를 구체적으로 쓰지 않고 'after World War II', 'by the 1970s' 수준으로만 적었습니다.
케이블식 굴착기 제조사 중 살아남은 회사 수는 책에 구체적 수치가 있으나 정확히 확인하지 못해 카드에는 'most'로만 썼습니다. 게시 전 원문 수치를 확인하고 필요하면 반영하세요.
초기 유압식 굴착기가 트랙터에 부착되어 소규모 업체의 배수로·도랑 작업에 쓰였다는 설명은 Christensen의 서술을 요약한 것입니다. 원문 표현과 맞는지 확인하세요.
King & Baatartogtokh(2015)는 Christensen이 든 사례 다수가 이론의 조건을 모두 충족하지는 않는다고 평가했습니다. 카드에는 구체적 비율 없이 일반적으로만 언급했습니다.
8번 카드의 회계 소프트웨어 회사와 월 $15 앱은 설명용 가상 사례입니다.

cards.title: Why well-run companies lose to worse products
body: After World War II, a group of companies built the giant cable-driven shovels that dug mines, canals and city foundations. They knew their customers well and kept making their machines bigger and better.
Most of them still disappeared. The machine that beat them was, at first, smaller and weaker.

image.label: A giant cable shovel beside a small hydraulic digger
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 거대한 케이블식 굴착기(와이어와 붐이 보이는 구형 기계), 오른쪽에 트랙터에 붙은 작은 유압식 굴착기가 도랑을 파는 모습. 실제 제조사 로고나 색상 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you put next year's budget?
body: You make large cable shovels. Your best customers, miners and big contractors, want bigger buckets and longer reach. They pay well.
A new hydraulic digger has appeared. It's small, digs trenches for little local builders, and sells at thin margins. Your best customers say it's useless for their work.

options.text: Build bigger shovels for the customers who pay the most
options.feedback: You keep your best customers happy this year. But you ignore the product that is improving fastest, and it may reach your market later.

options.text: Add a hydraulic model to your main line, sold by your current sales team
options.feedback: You get the technology in-house. But your sales team will push it to miners who don't want it, and it will lose every budget fight to the big machines.

options.text: Set up a small separate team to sell hydraulic diggers to small builders
options.feedback: You give up some focus and accept low margins for a while. In return, the new product gets customers who actually want it and a team that cares about small wins.

cards.title: The weak machine kept getting stronger.
body: Early hydraulic diggers could only handle small buckets. So they were sold to small builders, often mounted on tractors, for digging ditches. The big shovel makers' customers had no use for them.
The incumbents did what good managers do. They served their best customers and invested in their most profitable products.
Meanwhile, hydraulic machines improved year after year. By the 1970s they could handle much of the work cable shovels did. Most cable shovel makers did not survive the shift.

cards.title: The innovator's dilemma
body: The **innovator's dilemma** is a trap for successful companies: the habits that make them succeed are the same habits that make them miss the next big shift.

Clayton Christensen named it in his 1997 book. His surprise finding was that leaders often failed *because* they were well managed. Listening to your best customers and chasing higher margins is usually wise. With a disruptive product, it points you the wrong way.

cards.title: Three good habits that turn into a trap.
body: When a weaker, cheaper product appears, sensible rules push leaders to pass on it.
list: **Listen to your best customers:** they don't want it, so it looks like a bad idea
**Go after big markets:** its first market is tiny and can't move a large company's growth
**Protect your margins:** its low profits look worse than your core products
cards.callout: Each rule is right on its own. Together they guarantee you arrive late.
cards.softwareNote: The same trap catches software leaders. Big customers ask for more features, while a simpler, cheaper app quietly wins users the leader never served.

cards.title: Give the new thing its own home.
body: Christensen's main advice: put the disruptive product in a separate, small unit. It needs its own customers, its own prices and its own way of measuring success.
A small team gets excited about a small market. It can live with low margins because its costs are built for them. It doesn't have to win budget fights against the core business every quarter.

image.label: A small team in its own building next to a large factory
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 큰 공장 건물("Core business") 옆에 작은 별도 건물("New unit"). 각 건물 아래에 "Big customers · High margins"와 "New customers · Low margins" 라벨. 두 건물은 얇은 선 하나로만 연결.

cards.title: Not every cheap upstart is a threat.
body: Many low-end products stay low-end. If you chase every one, you waste money and distract your team.

The theory also has critics. Historian Jill Lepore and researchers Andrew King and Baljir Baatartogtokh argued that many famous examples don't fit it neatly, and that it's easier to spot disruption in hindsight.
The useful question isn't "is this cheap?" It's "is it improving fast enough to reach my customers?"

cards.title: Now it's accounting software.
body: Your software serves mid-size firms on annual contracts, set up by consultants. A startup sells a simple $15-a-month app for freelancers. It lacks features your clients need, and they laugh at it.
Its user base is growing fast, and it adds features every month. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it. Your best clients say it's no threat
options.feedback: Your clients are right about today. But they can't tell you how good the app will be in three years, and by then catching up costs far more.

options.text: Add a cheap "lite" plan sold by your current sales team
options.feedback: It's quick and cheap to launch. But reps paid on big contracts won't push a $15 plan, and it will be judged by your core margins.

options.text: Fund a small team with its own pricing that targets freelancers
options.feedback: It costs money and may compete with you a little. But it lets you learn the new market while the startup is still small.

cards.title: Your best customers can lead you away from your future.
body: Good management rules work for improving what you sell. They fail when a weaker product starts improving faster than your customers' needs.
**Try it today:** name one cheap, "not good enough" rival your best customers dismiss. Write down how much it improved in the last year.
